'''Yasuji Okada''' (born 1968) is a Japanese molecular biologist and physician. He is a professor at the [[University of Tokyo]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=OKADA Yasushi |url=https://www.s.u-tokyo.ac.jp/en/people/okada_yasushi/ |access-date=2024-04-19 |website=SCHOOL OF SCIENCE THE UNIVERSITY OF TOKYO |language=en}}</ref> He is known for his research in single-molecule biology and bioimage informatics, notably discovering that kinesin can move as a single molecule. Collaborating with Olympus, he also developed a high-speed, high-resolution spinning disk [[super-resolution microscopy]] technique.<ref>{{Cite web |title=オリンパス ニュースリリース： 超解像蛍光顕微鏡法の新技術を理化学研究所と共同開発 |url=https://www.olympus.co.jp/jp/news/2015a/nr150415microj.html |access-date=2024-04-19 |website=www.olympus.co.jp |language=ja}}</ref> He is the chief researcher at the University of Tokyo's International Research Centre for Neurointelligence, leading the ''Information Physics of Living Matters project''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Members – Planned Research |url=https://infophys-bio.jp/wpen/soshiki |access-date=2024-04-19 |website=Information physics of living matters |language=ja}}</ref> This project had already secured 1.15 billion yen (approximately US$10 million) of government research grant before it started.<ref>“[https://kaken.nii.ac.jp/ja/file/KAKENHI-AREA-8104/8104_saitaku_gaiyo_ja.pdf 8104 研究概要 (採択時)]”. ''KAKEN 科学研究費助成事業データベース''. 国立情報学研究所. 2020年8月22日閲覧。</ref>

== Career ==
Okada entered Nada Junior High School in 1981 and Nada High School in 1984. Commuting by train from his home in [[Osaka]], he spent his travel time reading extensively. During his high school years, he read "Mechanics" by [[Landau and Lifshitz (book)|Landau and Lifshitz]], part of the Course of Theoretical Physics series, and "[[The Feynman Lectures on Physics]]".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-08-06 |title=世の中、上には上がいる〜私が見た「大秀才」たち（週刊現代） @gendai_biz |url=http://gendai.media/articles/-/20944 |access-date=2024-04-19 |website=現代ビジネス |language=ja}}</ref>

In 1987, Okada matriculated at the University of Tokyo. Facing a decision in his second year there between the Medical School and the Department of Biochemistry in the Faculty of Science (''[[University of Tokyo#Junior division|Shinfuri]]''), he chose Medicine following advice from [[Yoshinori Ohsumi]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=第42回 {{!}} この人に聞く「生命に関わる仕事っておもしろいですか？」 {{!}} 中高生と"いのちの不思議"を考える─生命科学DOKIDOKI研究室 |url=https://www.terumozaidan.or.jp/labo/interview/42/02.html |access-date=2024-04-19 |website=www.terumozaidan.or.jp}}</ref> He began his doctoral studies in 1993. He focused on single-molecule biology using specialised optical microscopy to visualise the physical movements of individual molecules. While the prevailing theory was that [[Kinesin|kinesin motor]] proteins worked like two-legged walking, Okada discovered cases where a single molecule could move independently.<ref>{{Cite web |title=第42回 {{!}} この人に聞く「生命に関わる仕事っておもしろいですか？」 {{!}} 中高生と"いのちの不思議"を考える─生命科学DOKIDOKI研究室 |url=https://www.terumozaidan.or.jp/labo/interview/42/03.html |access-date=2024-04-19 |website=www.terumozaidan.or.jp}}</ref> Okada's doctoral thesis was titled "[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10024239/ The motility mechanism of the single-headed kinesin motor, KIF1A]".

Around 2005, he and his graduate students discovered the role of Kinesin-2, cilia, and flagella in determining the left-right asymmetry of the heart, a condition referred to as [[situs inversus]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=夢プロフェッショナル 〜夢を叶えるプロフェッショナルたちの挑戦〜 {{!}} すべて自分で「見たんか？」が信条 |url=http://www.qbic.riken.jp/japanese/dream/okada/ |access-date=2024-04-19 |website=www.qbic.riken.jp}}</ref>

In 2015, in collaboration with [[Olympus Corporation]], he developed a super-resolution [[fluorescence microscope]] with approximately 100 nanometers spatial resolution and 10 milliseconds [[temporal resolution]], named "spinning disk super-resolution microscopy". This technique was noted for being a hundred times faster than existing super-resolution microscopy methods and achieved the world's fastest shutter speed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=オリンパス ニュースリリース： 超解像蛍光顕微鏡法の新技術を理化学研究所と共同開発 |url=https://www.olympus.co.jp/jp/news/2015a/nr150415microj.html |access-date=2024-04-19 |website=www.olympus.co.jp |language=ja}}</ref>
